deck.title: Reliable Robotic Manipulation Through Evidence-Grounded PID and Fuzzy-PID Evaluation

slides.title: Reliable control enables action
slides.subtitle: Evidence-grounded PID and Fuzzy-PID evaluation for a 2-link manipulator
slides.figureAlt: MATLAB and Simscape Multibody end-effector tracking comparison
slides.presenterNote: Frame the project as a validated execution layer rather than an end-to-end robot intelligence stack.

slides.title: Nominal success does not prove reliable manipulation
slides.claim: Controller choice must survive changes in payload, configuration, noise, disturbance, and actuator authority.
body: A controller can pass one nominal trajectory and still fail when uncertainties interact.
This study therefore reports failed completed runs instead of filtering them from averages.
All conclusions are simulation-only; no hardware safety or fidelity claim is made.
slides.figureAlt: Nominal PID and Fuzzy-PID joint tracking comparison
slides.presenterNote: Use the nominal plot to motivate why the later stress matrix is necessary.

slides.title: Every controller follows the same protocol
slides.interpretation: Manual PID, Mamdani Fuzzy-PID, and optimized PID use identical robot parameters, torque limits, trajectories, thresholds, and random seeds.
slides.presenterNote: Emphasize fairness before discussing controller rankings.

slides.title: Optimization improves PID under a fixed protocol
slides.claim: Optimization lowers the nominal objective 7.283% and the held-out payload objective from 0.214504 to 0.197284.
body: The search converges with exit flag 1 after 12 iterations and 96 evaluations.
Only PID gains change; the plant, torque limits, trajectory, objective, and evaluation thresholds remain fixed.
slides.presenterNote: Separate tuning evidence from reliability evidence: a lower objective does not prove universal robustness.

slides.title: Deterministic stress separates controller reliability
slides.claim: Success rises from 8/13 for manual PID to 9/13 for Fuzzy-PID and 10/13 for optimized PID.
body: The matrix contains 39 controller-scenario runs across nominal, payload, configuration, uncertainty, disturbance, actuator, and combined conditions.
All 3 controllers fail the combined deterministic case, so the ranking is comparative rather than a safety guarantee.
slides.figureAlt: Deterministic robustness success counts and error summary
slides.presenterNote: State both the aggregate ranking and the shared combined-condition failure.

slides.title: Noise alone is manageable; combined stress is not
slides.claim: Each isolated-noise cell passes 30/30 paired trials, while every combined-stress cell passes 0/30.
body: Study: 360 trials (4 scenarios x 3 controllers x 30 fixed seeds).
At high noise, optimized PID has the lowest tracking error but the highest mean torque slew (2888.34 N m/s).
slides.presenterNote: Use the paired-seed design to explain why the controller comparison is fair.

slides.title: Task-space tests expose hidden failures
slides.claim: All 3 controllers pass straight-line; only optimized PID passes pick-transfer-place, so 4 of 6 task runs pass every gate.
body: Manual and Fuzzy-PID complete the pick-transfer-place simulation but fail its quantitative pickup/place criteria.
Optimized PID records 0.01422 m RMS and 0.02970 m maximum Cartesian error.
slides.presenterNote: Completed does not mean successful; retain the 2 failed completed runs.

slides.title: Independent formulations agree numerically
slides.interpretation: The result supports model consistency under one fixed protocol. Shared parameters and target trajectories mean it is not evidence of hardware fidelity.
slides.presenterNote: Distinguish independent formulation from independent physical validation.

slides.title: Optimized PID is the strongest reliability baseline
slides.interpretation: Nominal metrics are mixed across manual PID and Fuzzy-PID; optimized PID provides the best aggregate deterministic and Cartesian reliability, with a torque-slew trade-off under noise.
slides.presenterNote: Deliver a conditional conclusion, not a universal-controller claim.

slides.title: Validated layer supports the next research step
slides.claim: The next milestone is to test whether the same evidence discipline survives contact with sensing, hardware uncertainty, and online safety constraints.
body: 1. Hardware-in-the-loop and physical-arm validation with calibrated uncertainty.
2. Perception and task-planning integration above the existing inner-loop controller layer.
3. Online monitoring, collision avoidance, and explicit safety supervision before deployment.
slides.presenterNote: Close by resolving the opening: the low-level layer is validated for simulation and bounded next research is clear.

summary.title: Reliable Robotic Manipulation Through Evidence-Grounded Control
summary.takeaway: Across identical simulation protocols, optimized PID produced the strongest aggregate reliability while no controller dominated every condition.
summary.problem: Reliable manipulation requires more than nominal trajectory tracking: controllers must remain interpretable under payload, configuration, disturbance, noise, and actuator changes.
summary.method: A 2-link arm compares manual PID, Mamdani Fuzzy-PID, and bounded optimization-assisted PID under identical 0.001 s simulation, trajectory, torque-limit, threshold, and paired-seed protocols.

results.label: per controller-scenario cell: isolated-noise cell vs full-combined-stress cell

summary.figureCaption: Deterministic stress testing separates aggregate controller reliability while preserving failed cases.
summary.significance: The project supplies a transparent low-level execution layer that can sit beneath future perception, language, and task-planning systems.
summary.limitations: Simulation only; no hardware fidelity, collision avoidance, perception, online safety supervisor, or end-to-end embodied-AI implementation is claimed.
summary.nextSteps: Validate on hardware, add calibrated sensing uncertainty, and introduce runtime safety monitoring before deployment claims.
